headings.text: Two TLSOptions: optional vs strict client auth
Shared-secret plumbing: Validity-Secret across namespaces and phases
Known limitation: the validity check is the interim revocation mechanism

blocks.html:
⚠️ Closed alpha — provisional docs. OpenDefence on Kubernetes (opendefence-platform) is in closed alpha and under rapid, breaking development. This page describes a moving target and will most likely be superseded by the documentation that ships with the first public release — treat everything here as provisional, and do not rely on it for a production deployment.

This page traces how a client certificate presented at the edge becomes a set of trusted identity headers on the request that reaches a backend: two Traefik TLSOption resources terminate mutual TLS, and a chain of three in-repo Traefik plugins turns the verified certificate into Callsign / Callsign-Valid headers, checking the callsign against rmapi on every request. It is for developers and operators who need to understand or debug the edge identity path in pvarki/opendefence-platform. How the client certificates are issued is covered in PKI & trust; how to put this protection in front of your own integration is covered in Register your integration (Kubernetes).

Two TLSOptions: optional vs strict client auth

Client-certificate termination is configured with two Traefik TLSOption resources in k8s/opendefence-system/overlays/{local,cloud}/mtls.tlsoption.yaml (namespace opendefence-system). Both trust the same ca-bundle secret — the platform root + intermediate CA public certs that trust-manager syncs into every namespace (see PKI & trust) — and differ only in enforcement:

TLSOption clientAuthType Behaviour
mtls-optional VerifyClientCertIfGiven Handshake succeeds without a cert; if one is presented it must verify against ca-bundle
mtls-strict RequireAndVerifyClientCert Handshake fails outright without a valid cert

apiVersion: traefik.io/v1alpha1
kind: TLSOption
metadata:
  name: mtls-strict
  namespace: opendefence-system
spec:
  clientAuth:
    secretNames:
    - ca-bundle
    clientAuthType: RequireAndVerifyClientCert

Routes in other namespaces (app-tak, app-mtx, …) reference these options — and the traefik-system middlewares below — via Traefik's cross-namespace mode; see Ingress & network edge.

The hosts that carry a client-cert chain, per docs/endpoints.md and the per-app IngressRoute manifests (the full hostname map, and the <domain> definition, live in Ingress & network edge):

Host Client cert Chain middleware on the routes
mtls.<domain> mtls-optional mtls-chain on the UI root, mtls-chain-with-legacy on rmapi /api; product UIs under /ui/tak, /ui/mtx, /ui/matrix carry no chain
tak.<domain> mtls-optional mtls-chain-with-legacy on /api; /ephemeral/api gets only mtls-legacy-client-cert-headers
bl.<domain> mtls-strict mtls-chain
mtx.<domain> mtls-strict mtls-chain-with-legacy on /api
matrix.<domain> mtls-strict mtls-chain-with-legacy on /api

The split follows a simple rule: machine-to-machine integration APIs (bl., mtx., matrix.) are mtls-strict — a client without a cert has no business there and gets a TLS failure. Hosts a browser may reach in a half-configured state (mtls.<domain>, tak.<domain>) are mtls-optional, so the handshake completes even without a cert and the callsign-redirect middleware can answer with a friendly error page instead of a raw TLS alert.

Two things this machinery deliberately does not cover: kc.<domain>:9443 bypasses Traefik entirely (Keycloak terminates its own TLS with --https-client-auth=request built into the image), and the raw TCP/UDP product ports (TAK CoT streaming, MediaMTX streams, LiveKit media) never pass through the websecure entrypoint — see Ingress & network edge. The callsign check applies only to HTTPS routes on port 443.

The mtls-chain plugin pipeline

Verifying the certificate chain only proves the cert was issued by the platform CA. Turning it into a per-request authorization decision — is this callsign still valid right now? — is done by three small Go plugins vendored in-repo at k8s/traefik/base/plugins/{callsign-validity,callsign-redirect,legacy-mtls-headers}/. They load through Traefik's experimental.localPlugins mechanism — an experimental Traefik feature in which the Yaegi interpreter executes the plugin Go source at startup; no compiled artifacts, no external plugin registry. The base kustomization packs each plugin's go.mod, .traefik.yml and plugin.go into a ConfigMap (traefik-local-plugin-callsignvalidity-source and siblings) mounted into the Traefik pod at /plugins-local/src/github.com/pvarki/traefik-<plugin-dir-name> (e.g. traefik-callsign-validity).

What each plugin does, in pipeline order:

  1. **callsign-validity** (middleware callsign-validity, defined in k8s/traefik/middleware/base/) — reads the CN of the verified client leaf certificate (req.TLS.VerifiedChains; a cert that was presented but not verified counts as no cert). It first authoritatively resets its output headers, then POSTs {"callsign": "<CN>"} to http://rmapi.opendefence-system.svc.cluster.local:8000/api/v1/internal/callsign-validity/check with the shared secret in a Validity-Secret header (3 s timeout). It records the verdict in Callsign (the CN), Callsign-Valid (true/false) and Callsign-Valid-Reason (ok / no_cert / invalid / error, where error means rmapi was unreachable or answered abnormally). It always forwards — policy lives downstream, in one place.
  2. **callsign-redirect** (middleware callsign-redirect) — the single decision point. Callsign-Valid: true forwards unchanged. Otherwise it maps the reason to an error code (invalid → unauthorized, no_cert → mtls_fail, error → generic error page) and: on an mtls.<baseDomain> host it 302-redirects to the base domain at /error?code=…; on any other host it returns a bare 403, so an invalid verdict never reaches a protected backend.
  3. **legacy-mtls-headers** (middleware mtls-legacy-client-cert-headers) — sets X-ClientCert-DN (subject DN) and X-ClientCert-Serial (uppercase hex) for backends ported from the legacy Compose stack, and deletes both when no verified cert is present.

A fourth, built-in middleware mtls-pass-client-cert (Traefik's passTLSClientCert: serial number plus subject CN/O) runs first in every chain and feeds X-Forwarded-Tls-Client-Cert-Info to backends that parse certificate info themselves.

The full life of a request through the edge, from handshake to backend:

blocks.code:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Browser
    participant Traefik
    participant rmapi
    participant Backend
    Browser->>Traefik: HTTPS request with client certificate
    Note over Traefik: handshake verifies the cert against ca-bundle per the route TLSOption
    Note over Traefik: strip-identity-headers clears every client-sent identity header
    Note over Traefik: mtls-pass-client-cert and legacy-mtls-headers annotate the request
    Traefik->>rmapi: POST /api/v1/internal/callsign-validity/check with Validity-Secret header
    rmapi-->>Traefik: JSON verdict, valid true or false
    Note over Traefik: callsign-validity sets Callsign, Callsign-Valid, Callsign-Valid-Reason
    alt Callsign-Valid is true
        Traefik->>Backend: forward with trusted identity headers
    else invalid on an mtls host
        Traefik-->>Browser: 302 to base domain /error?code=unauthorized
    else invalid on any other host
        Traefik-->>Browser: 403 Forbidden
    end

blocks.html: The plugins are composed into two chain middlewares that routes attach: mtls-chain (mtls-pass-client-cert → callsign-validity → callsign-redirect) and mtls-chain-with-legacy, which inserts mtls-legacy-client-cert-headers after the pass-cert step. Execution order across a request:

blocks.html:
One repo-layout wrinkle: callsign-validity and strip-identity-headers live in k8s/traefik/middleware/base/, but mtls-middlewares.yaml (the pass-cert, legacy-headers, redirect and both chain definitions) lives in k8s/traefik/middleware/overlays/{local,cloud}/, because callsign-redirect needs an environment-specific baseDomain — hard-coded localmaeher.dev.pvarki.fi locally, the Zarf-templated OPENDEFENCE_HOST in cloud. The middleware CRs are applied with the opendefence phase, while Traefik itself and the plugin-source ConfigMaps ship in infra-phase1 (see Deployment model).

Header hygiene: the anti-spoofing contract

None of the above would be trustworthy if a client could simply send Callsign-Valid: true itself. The strip-identity-headers middleware (k8s/traefik/middleware/base/strip-identity-headers-middleware.yaml) is attached as a default entrypoint middleware on websecure in the Traefik Helm values (traefik-system-strip-identity-headers@kubernetescrd), so it runs on every 443 request before any router middleware. It unconditionally removes every client-supplied identity header — in Traefik, an empty customRequestHeaders value deletes the header:

X-ClientCert-DN, X-ClientCert-Serial, X-SSL-Client-Verify, X-SSL-Client-Fingerprint, Callsign, Callsign-Valid, Callsign-Valid-Reason, l5d-client-id, X-Forwarded-Tls-Client-Cert, X-Forwarded-Tls-Client-Cert-Info, Validity-Secret.

This is the contract downstream apps rely on: if a request arrived through the edge, any of these headers it carries were set by Traefik's own middleware, never by the client. Stripping Validity-Secret prevents replaying the shared secret at rmapi's internal check endpoint through the edge, and stripping l5d-client-id keeps the Linkerd-set mesh identity header equally unforgeable (see Service mesh (Linkerd)). As defence in depth, the callsign-validity plugin also resets the Callsign* headers itself before evaluating, so even a route that somehow missed the entrypoint default would not pass spoofed verdicts through the chain.

Shared-secret plumbing: Validity-Secret across namespaces and phases

The Validity-Secret header authenticates Traefik to rmapi's internal check endpoint. Both ends read the same generated secret, but they run in different namespaces; the k8s/_shared/traefik-secret-mirror kustomize Component bridges the gap:

  • Source (k8s/opendefence-system/base/resources/callsign-validity-shared-secret.yaml, applied in the opendefence phase): an External Secrets Operator Password generator (password-32-8digits-no-symbols) mints a 32-character password once (refreshInterval: "0") into Secret callsign-validity-shared-secret in opendefence-system. The rmapi Deployment consumes it directly as env RM_CALLSIGN_VALIDITY_SECRET.
  • Mirror (_shared/traefik-secret-mirror, applied in infra-phase2): ESO copies the secret into traefik-system under the same name — the cross-namespace mirror recipe, this instance included, is diagrammed in Data & secrets.
  • Consumer: the Traefik Deployment (from infra-phase1) takes env RM_CALLSIGN_VALIDITY_SECRET from the mirrored secret with optional: false; the callsign-validity middleware names that env via sharedSecretEnv.

The cross-phase subtlety: Traefik (phase 1) references a secret whose mirror machinery only arrives in phase 2, and whose source only exists once the opendefence phase applies. There is no explicit ordering gate for this — on a fresh install the Traefik container simply cannot start (optional: false) until the source secret exists and ESO has completed a mirror cycle; the system converges through ESO reconciliation (~20 s) and kubelet retries rather than through the taskfile's rollout gates. It works, but it is eventual consistency by design — a Traefik pod stuck in CreateContainerConfigError early in an install is usually this dependency, not a Traefik problem.

Known limitation: the validity check is the interim revocation mechanism

Per the repo README, certificate revocation checking (OCSP) is currently disabled in Keycloak and TAK (TAK_OCSP_ENABLE is "false"), so at those layers a revoked certificate keeps working. The per-request callsign-validity check against rmapi is the interim revocation enforcement: rmapi answers valid: false for a revoked or unknown callsign and callsign-redirect blocks the request at the edge — but anything that bypasses the websecure entrypoint (Keycloak on 9443, TAK's raw TCP ports) does not get this check. A fix is in progress: rmapi is slated to serve its own OCSP responses (its RM_OCSCP_RESPONDER env already points at the base domain), after which OCSP checking will be re-enabled in the consumers.
